turns.content:
Hey, can I get a completely honest read on something? Last night at dinner my partner Leo used "they" for my brother Julian three separate times. Julian went quiet and left early. I could see it land on him each time. I wrote a draft text this morning: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters." 

I'm not asking for a rewrite. I just need to know — does that sound too sharp? Or am I underreacting by texting instead of talking about it in person?

It doesn’t sound cruel. It also doesn’t sound like nothing.

The sharpness isn’t volume — it’s the tally plus the correction. “Three times” plus “He’s a man” reads less like a request and more like a grade. Even if both are true, that’s the part that’ll make Leo brace instead of listen. “I know you mean well but it matters” is trying to soften it, and it still comes off a little like a pat on the head.

You’re not underreacting by caring. You might be underselling it by putting it in a text.

Julian went quiet and left early. You watched it hit him. That’s not a grammar note you drop in the morning. A text makes it easy to send and easy for Leo to treat as a one-line oops. In person (or at least a call) you can say what actually happened — that it landed, that your brother shut down — and you can tell whether this was a sloppy habit or something Leo thinks is the respectful default.

So: not too sharp to be fair. A bit sharp in the wrong places. And texting is the lighter move than the night probably earned. If you only do one thing, talk. The ask can stay simple. The medium should match the fact that someone left the table.

That's fair. I think I was trying to sound matter-of-fact so it wouldn't feel like an attack, but "He's a man" does read like a correction. Not a request.

~I don't know. I'm worried if I talk in person I'll say something worse. I was already clenching my jaw at the table. That's partly why I wrote it down.

EDIT: I'm not sure if the text being sharp is actually a problem or if I'm just uncomfortable that I'm mad at Leo. He's not a bad guy. He's been great with Julian otherwise.

You’re not crazy for writing it down. Jaw clenched at the table is a real reason to not improvise later. That’s you trying not to make it worse, not you being a coward.

The EDIT is the actual thing. The text being a little sharp is not the main problem. You being uncomfortable that you’re mad at Leo is.

He’s not a villain. He can still have done something that landed, three times, in front of your brother, who then left. Those two facts can sit next to each other. “He’s been great otherwise” is why this is worth saying carefully. It is not a reason to pretend it didn’t happen.

A text isn’t automatically wrong. It’s wrong if the point of it is to get the anger out of your body without having to watch his face. It’s also wrong if you sand it down so much he hears “tiny preference” instead of “Julian went quiet and left.”

You don’t have to choose between a sharp text and an unfiltered fight. Use the draft as a script, not a missile. Talk when your jaw isn’t still locked. Keep it to what you saw: he used they, it hit Julian, please use he/him. You can skip the scorekeeping and the “he’s a man” line. You don’t have to skip that it mattered.

Being mad at someone you like is allowed. That’s not the same as needing to sound angry to be taken seriously.

I keep coming back to the "He's a man" line. You're right, it reads like a grade. I think I put that in because I'm afraid he doesn't actually see Julian that way.

~I don't know. Maybe I'm overcomplicating it.

EDIT: The line I'm stuck on is "Please just use he/him." Does that sound like I'm telling him off, or is it clear enough?

“Please just use he/him” is the clearest line in the draft. It’s not the one that sounds like a scolding.

The only word doing extra work is **just**. “Please use he/him” is a request. “Please *just* use he/him” can land as “this is simple, stop making it a thing.” That’s a light edge, not a blowup. On its own, it’s fine. It only starts to feel like telling him off when it sits next to the tally and “He’s a man.”

You’re not overcomplicating the wording. You’re circling the fear underneath it.

“He’s a man” wasn’t there to be precise. It was there because you’re not sure Leo actually sees Julian that way. A pronoun ask can fix the words at dinner. It cannot answer that. That’s why that line keeps tugging at you, and why “Please just use he/him” feels too small for what you’re actually worried about.

If the only job of the text is “use he/him,” that line is clear enough. If the job is “I need to know you see my brother as a man,” that’s a different conversation, and it probably shouldn’t live in a morning text.

You can be mad at someone who’s otherwise been good. Those aren’t competing facts.
Okay. So if I cut "He's a man" and just lead with what I saw — that Julian went quiet and left — does that take the edge off enough? Or does it make it sound like I'm guilt-tripping him?

It takes the *correction* edge off. It can still sound like a guilt trip if that’s the opening and the whole weight of the night.

“He’s a man” grades Leo. “Julian went quiet and left” shows the cost. That’s a better reason to speak up. It’s also a heavier image, so if you lead with it, Leo may hear “you made him leave” before he hears “please use he/him.”

The difference is pretty small on the page:

- Impact: I saw it land. He went quiet and left early. Please use he/him.
- Guilt: You did this, he left because of you, sit with that.

You don’t need to prosecute the three times *and* the early exit. One concrete thing you saw is enough. Don’t claim you know the whole reason he left unless you’re sure. “I could see it land, and then he went quiet / left early” is honest. “You drove him out” is a charge.

It also still doesn’t answer the thing you’re actually scared of — whether Leo sees Julian as a man. This version just asks for the behavior and names why it mattered at the table. That’s the right size for a text. The bigger fear is a conversation, not a morning message.

So: yes, cut “He’s a man.” Name what you saw, then make the ask. If you lead with the leaving, keep it short so it doesn’t become the point of the text.

Okay. That makes sense. Keep it concrete, not a charge.

I think I'm ready to send it. One last check — does the timing feel okay? Sending it today, the morning after? Or should I wait until tonight when we can actually talk?

Same day is right. First thing this morning is not.

A morning-after text about last night is normal. A 6 a.m. one about your brother leaving the table is not. He’ll read it before he’s a person, and then you both spend the whole day inside a thread. That’s how a clear ask turns into a fight about tone.

If you can actually talk tonight, wait and talk. Use the draft as notes, not as a send. That’s the version that matches what happened.

If you need it out of your body before then, don’t send the whole thing. Send a placeholder: you want to talk tonight about dinner. That’s not backing down. That’s not letting the day turn into a silent movie.

Don’t wait longer than tonight. Sitting on it until it becomes a speech is how you say something worse.
